architecture.mechanism: Coupled hydrothermal finite-element simulation of temperature and pressure fields can predict the hydrothermal conditions that drive mineral solubility, enabling operators to identify where flashed brine crosses into calcite/silica supersaturation and to shift operating conditions off the scaling envelope before deposition nucleates on internals.
architecture.intervention: Build a calibrated reduced-order hydrothermal FE replica of the existing wellhead flash train and cyclone separators (clamp-on sensors and external modeling only, no pressure-boundary welding, geometry matched to the installed vessels), then use it to re-tune flash pressure, brine temperature drop, and injection-header flow paths so the brine's pressure-temperature trajectory stays below the calcite and silica gel saturation thresholds at the exact internal locations where scale currently forms.
architecture.expected_effect: Deposition onset on separator internals and injection headers is pushed well beyond the current 45-60 day window, and the quarterly 6-11 percent thermal output loss shrinks as flow area and heat-transfer surface remain clean between maintenance cycles.
architecture.falsification_test: Run the simulator against historical field data and check whether it reproduces the observed 45-60 day calcite onset and the downstream silica gel zoning; then implement the re-tuned flash conditions in a single pilot well and measure scale mass on removable coupons and separator pressure drop over two quarters, comparing against the eleven unchanged wells as control.
